title: Disagreement, a history: open data

teloi.name: Truth
teloi.gloss: Disagreement is a symptom of error; the exchange exists to remove it. Winning is incidental.

teloi.name: Victory
teloi.gloss: The exchange is a contest. Its product is a winner, a reputation, or an audience persuaded.

teloi.name: Formation
teloi.gloss: Disputation as gymnasium: the point is the trained disputant, not the settled question.

teloi.name: Decision
teloi.gloss: A collective must act; disagreement is processed into a binding choice without being dissolved.

teloi.name: Settlement
teloi.gloss: Parties want different things; the exchange seeks terms both can accept.

teloi.name: Understanding
teloi.gloss: The exchange aims at accurate mutual comprehension and repaired relation; agreement is optional.

teloi.name: Plurality
teloi.gloss: Disagreement is to be preserved, recorded and honoured; closure is a loss.

teloi.name: Release
teloi.gloss: The goal is to be freed from the grip of positions: suspension, emptiness, the hinge of the Way.

domains.name: Epistemic
domains.gloss: It is really about what is true: evidence, inference, priors, perspective.

domains.name: Linguistic
domains.gloss: It is really about words: names, equivocation, attitudes dressed as beliefs, idioms with no common measure.

domains.name: Axiological
domains.gloss: It is really about values: rival goods, sacred commitments, incommensurable gods.

domains.name: Interest
domains.gloss: It is really about what people want: stakes, resources, bargaining positions.

domains.name: Power
domains.gloss: It is really about who rules: domination, hegemony, sovereignty, the friend and the enemy.

domains.name: Psyche
domains.gloss: It is really about what is happening inside: needs, fear, vanity, envy, motivated cognition, developmental form.

domains.name: Relational
domains.gloss: It is really about us: identity, recognition, the relationship-level message beneath the content.

domains.name: Contemplative
domains.gloss: It is really about attachment: clinging to views, a self that needs to be right, partial sight of a whole.

domains.name: Generative
domains.gloss: It is not a problem at all: disagreement is the engine of truth, history, sociation or law.

methods.name: Antilogic
methods.summary: Protagoras was reported to be the first to say that on every matter there are two logoi opposed to each other. Antilogic is the drill that follows: argue the case, then argue its contrary with equal force. Its premise is the homo-mensura doctrine. If each person is the measure, then disagreement is not a defect to be cured but the normal condition of speech, and the trained speaker learns to make the weaker logos the stronger.
moves: Pair every speech with its counter-speech
Treat the audience as the measure of success
Exploit the reversibility of commonplaces (good/bad, just/unjust)
methods.note: Plato’s whole project can be read as a refusal of antilogic that keeps borrowing its tools.
methods.third_party: The audience, who judge which logos prevails.
methods.ends_well_when: The stronger speech wins the room.
methods.typical_failure: Cleverness detached from any care for truth.

critique.text: Rhetoric of this kind is a knack of flattery, not an art. It produces conviction without knowledge.

methods.name: Eristic
methods.when: late 5th c. BCE; satirised c. 380 BCE
methods.who: Euthydemus and Dionysodorus (as Plato portrays them)
methods.summary: Argument for the sake of winning. Any answer the respondent gives is turned into a refutation by equivocation, ambiguity or sheer pace. In the Euthydemus the brothers show that a learner both knows and does not know. Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations is in effect a field guide to eristic, written so that the dialectician can detect and defuse it.
moves: Ask questions whose every answer is a trap
Claim victory on any apparent contradiction
methods.note: Walton and Krabbe keep ‘eristic’ as a formal dialogue type: the quarrel, whose real goal is to hit the other party.
methods.ends_well_when: The opponent is reduced to silence or contradiction.
methods.typical_failure: Victory proves nothing; the question is never addressed.

critique.text: Eristic refutations only appear to be refutations. Name the fallacy and the victory evaporates.

methods.name: Socratic elenchus
methods.summary: The interlocutor states a thesis, usually a definition of a virtue. Socrates secures assent to further premises the interlocutor holds, then shows that these entail the thesis’s negation. The outcome is aporia, a stalled certainty. Vlastos’s ‘problem of the elenchus’ asks how exposing inconsistency could ever establish truth; the dialogues answer obliquely that what is examined is the person, not only the proposition.
moves: Ask for a definition (‘What is X?’)
Elicit the answerer’s own further beliefs
Derive contradiction; ask the answerer to revise
Say only what you believe (the ‘say what you think’ rule)
methods.note: Gorgias 458a: Socrates claims he would rather be refuted than refute, since being refuted rids one of the greater evil.
methods.third_party: None; bystanders sometimes, but the exchange is dyadic.
methods.ends_well_when: The answerer admits aporia and resolves to inquire further.
methods.typical_failure: Humiliation hardens the answerer instead of freeing them (Callicles, Thrasymachus).

critique.who: Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, ‘The Problem of Socrates’ §§5–7
critique.text: Dialectic is the weapon of those who have no other weapon: a plebeian revenge that forces the noble to prove themselves.

methods.name: Platonic dialectic
methods.summary: In the middle and late dialogues, dialectic becomes the capstone discipline. It runs by hypothesis upward to an unhypothetical first principle, and by collection and division: gather scattered instances under one form, then cut that form ‘at its natural joints’. Disagreement here is a symptom of failure to see the forms. The Republic bars dialectic to the young, who use argument like puppies tearing at whatever is near.
methods.third_party: None; the dialectician’s own vision of the forms.
methods.ends_well_when: Sight of the first principle; correct division of kinds.
methods.typical_failure: Closure: the philosopher who has seen the Good stops listening.

critique.who: Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945)
critique.text: A method that ends in certain vision licenses rule by those who claim to have it. Knowledge stays conjectural.

methods.name: Aristotelian dialectic
methods.summary: A rule-governed game between questioner and answerer, reasoning from endoxa: what is accepted by all, by most, or by the wise. The Topics catalogues the places (topoi) from which arguments may be drawn. Aristotle names three uses: intellectual exercise, encounters with ordinary people, and the philosophical sciences, where working through difficulties on both sides helps one see truth and falsity more easily.
moves: Answerer defends a thesis by yes/no replies
Questioner seeks to extract the contradictory
Diagnose sophisms by type (language vs. outside language)
methods.note: The dialectical game survives into the medieval obligationes and modern dialogue logic.
methods.third_party: Sometimes an examiner or audience in the Academy’s exercises.
methods.ends_well_when: The thesis survives examination, or the answerer is driven to contradiction.
methods.typical_failure: Argument from opinion never touches the world.

critique.text: The syllogism commands assent to propositions but not the thing itself. Discovery needs induction from experiment.

methods.name: Deliberative rhetoric
methods.summary: Rhetoric is the counterpart (antistrophos) of dialectic. It finds the available means of persuasion in matters that admit of being otherwise. In its deliberative genre an assembly is persuaded about future advantage. Disagreement is ordinary practical uncertainty, worked through by appeals of ēthos, pathos and logos before a crowd that cannot follow long chains of argument.
moves: Fit emotion to the decision at hand
methods.third_party: The assembly or jury, who decide.
methods.ends_well_when: A decision by the audience.
methods.typical_failure: Demagogy: emotion outruns judgment.

critique.text: Rhetoric produces belief without knowledge in a crowd that cannot test it.

methods.name: Stasis theory
methods.when: Hermagoras of Temnos, mid-2nd c. BCE
methods.summary: A procedure for finding where a dispute actually stands, the point at which the parties come to rest against each other. It asks four questions in order. Conjecture asks whether a thing was done. Definition asks what it should be called. Quality asks whether it was justified. Translation asks whether this forum has jurisdiction. Stasis theory is the oldest explicit taxonomy of what a disagreement is ‘really about’, and it already distinguishes the epistemic, the linguistic, the evaluative and the jurisdictional.
moves: Concede earlier stases to contest later ones
Shift the issue (translatio) when the forum is wrong
methods.note: Most quarrels are carried on at two different stases at once. One party argues fact while the other argues definition.
methods.third_party: Judge or court, whose jurisdiction is itself one of the stases.
methods.ends_well_when: The issue is located; the case is argued at the right stasis.
methods.typical_failure: Assumes a shared forum and law within which the issue can be placed.

critique.text: Some wrongs cannot be stated in the forum’s idiom. Stasis theory presupposes the common genre a differend lacks.

methods.name: Arguing both sides
methods.when: Arcesilaus c. 265 BCE; Carneades in Rome, 155 BCE
methods.summary: The sceptical Academy turned Socratic questioning into a standing practice of arguing for and against any thesis. On the Athenian embassy of 155 BCE Carneades argued for justice one day and against it the next, scandalising Cato. Cicero, who admired the method, said it suits the search for what is most probable and trains the orator in copiousness.
moves: Argue the thesis; argue its contrary
Withhold assent, or assent only to the persuasive (pithanon)
methods.third_party: None, or a pupil learning the method.
methods.ends_well_when: Assent to the most persuasive, held provisionally.
methods.typical_failure: Moral corrosion: arguing against justice weakens it.

critique.who: Cato the Elder, as reported by Plutarch, Cato Maior 22
critique.text: Send the philosophers home before the young learn to argue either side of justice.

methods.name: Pyrrhonian equipollence
methods.when: Pyrrho c. 300 BCE; Aenesidemus 1st c. BCE; Sextus c. 200 CE
methods.summary: Scepticism is ‘an ability to set out oppositions among things that appear and are thought of in any way at all’. Equal force on both sides yields suspension of judgment, and tranquillity follows ‘like a shadow’. Disagreement itself (diaphōnia) is the first of Agrippa’s five modes. Undecidable dispute among philosophers and ordinary people is a reason to suspend judgment, not to pick a side.
moves: Oppose appearance to appearance, thought to thought
Invoke the modes (dispute, regress, relativity, hypothesis, circularity)
methods.ends_well_when: Suspension of judgment, and with it tranquillity.
methods.typical_failure: Practical paralysis, or covert dogmatism about suspension itself.

critique.who: Hume, Enquiry concerning Human Understanding XII (1748)
critique.text: Pyrrhonism cannot survive action. Nature is too strong for principle, and the sceptic must still eat, act and believe.

methods.name: Refusing dispute
methods.when: among the oldest strata of the Pāli canon
methods.who: The Buddha of the Aṭṭhakavagga (Sutta Nipāta, ch. 4)
methods.summary: The sage does not enter disputes. Those who say ‘only this is pure’ and call the other a fool are bound by their views (diṭṭhi), and their debates yield only praise or blame and the anxiety of losing. Quarrels arise from what is held dear, and what is held dear from desire. Gómez reads this as a proto-Madhyamaka strand, a therapy of views rather than a better view.
moves: Decline to adopt a view to defend
Observe the craving behind the position
Let the dispute pass without taking a side
methods.ends_well_when: The sage does not take the dispute up.
methods.typical_failure: Error goes unchallenged; quietism.

critique.text: To protect true knowledge one must sometimes dispute, as a hedge of thorns protects a seedling.

methods.name: Abhidharma controversy
methods.when: trad. Third Council, c. 250 BCE; compiled over centuries
methods.summary: A canonical text of over two hundred points of controversy between the Theravāda and rival schools, set out as formalised exchanges. The orthodox questioner extracts an admission, then shows that it entails a contradiction with another admission. It is an early Indian dialogue-logic, structurally close to elenchus but used to police doctrinal boundaries.
moves: Close the point with the opponent’s self-contradiction
methods.third_party: The orthodox community that preserves the record.
methods.ends_well_when: The dissenting thesis is shown self-contradictory.
methods.typical_failure: The opponent never speaks in their own voice.

critique.text: The rival schools’ positions are reconstructed by the side that wins, so the controversy is staged.

methods.name: Vāda (good-faith debate)
methods.summary: The Nyāya-sūtra defines vāda as debate between parties who use the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the five-membered syllogism to establish or refute, without departing from an accepted doctrine. It is debate among teacher, pupil and peer, aimed at truth. The Caraka-saṃhitā likewise separates friendly discussion (sandhāya sambhāṣā) from hostile disputation and gives etiquette for each.
methods.third_party: Sometimes judges or a moderator (madhyastha) in public debate.
methods.ends_well_when: The thesis is established or refuted by pramāṇa.
methods.typical_failure: Agreement on the means of knowledge is assumed, not argued.

critique.text: If the means of knowledge establish objects, what establishes the means of knowledge? The regress has no end.

methods.name: Jalpa & vitaṇḍā
methods.summary: Jalpa is debate for victory, permitted to use quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti) and the opponent’s slips. Vitaṇḍā is jalpa without a counter-thesis: pure refutation. Nyāya permits both, as a hedge of thorns protecting the seedling of truth against unscrupulous opponents. This is a sober admission that good-faith procedures need a defence against bad faith.
methods.third_party: Judges and audience in public debate.
methods.ends_well_when: One side commits a point of defeat.
methods.typical_failure: Tricks win; truth loses.

critique.text: Defeat should come only from failing to prove one’s thesis, not from quibbles and sophistical rejoinders.

methods.name: Prasaṅga (reductio without thesis)
methods.summary: The Mādhyamika shows that each of the opponent’s positions entails absurdity, without advancing a position of its own. Pressed by Nyāya critics, Nāgārjuna answers: ‘If I had any thesis, that fault would apply to me. But I do not have any thesis.’ Formally this resembles vitaṇḍā. Its purpose is soteriological, the ‘pacification of conceptual proliferation’ (prapañcopaśama).
moves: Take the opponent’s view on its own terms
methods.ends_well_when: Every view is shown untenable; grasping ceases.
methods.typical_failure: Looks like nihilism or pure destructive cavil.

critique.text: A refutation that asserts nothing refutes nothing. Your denial is itself a thesis.

methods.name: Syādvāda (sevenfold predication)
methods.when: anekānta early; saptabhaṅgī systematised c. 5th–8th c. CE
methods.summary: Reality is many-sided (anekānta), so every assertion holds only ‘in some respect’ (syāt). The sevenfold scheme combines ‘is’, ‘is not’ and ‘is inexpressible’ under different standpoints (naya). Rival doctrines are recast as partial truths, each valid from its standpoint and false when absolutised. This is the elephant parable formalised as a logic.
moves: Index each claim to a standpoint
Map rival claims onto the seven predications
methods.ends_well_when: Each claim is indexed to its standpoint; the ‘only’ is dropped.
methods.typical_failure: Everything becomes partly true; no position can be wrong.

critique.text: Contradictory attributes cannot belong to one thing at once. A doctrine of ‘maybe’ yields no knowledge.

methods.name: Tibetan monastic debate
methods.when: Sangphu, 12th c.; Geluk curriculum to the present
methods.who: Chapa Chökyi Senge; Geluk monasteries (Sera, Drepung, Ganden)
methods.summary: A standing defender sits, and a challenger stands, claps and stamps on each point. The challenger presses consequences (thal ’gyur) built from the defender’s own answers. The defender may reply only ‘I accept’, ‘the reason is not established’ or ‘there is no pervasion’. Dreyfus describes it as hermeneutics through combat: a pedagogy of internalising a canon by being forced to defend it in public.
moves: Defender answers with one of three replies
Clap on each point; lineage-specific gestures mark defeat
methods.third_party: Assembled monks and the abbot, who watch and judge.
methods.ends_well_when: The defender holds the line or is forced to accept an absurd consequence.
methods.typical_failure: Virtuosity in defending a fixed curriculum, not inquiry.

critique.text: The courtyard trains the defence of orthodoxy; the canon is never itself in question.

methods.name: Mohist disputation
methods.summary: Canon A74: ‘disputation is contending over converse claims’. One party says ‘it is an ox’ and the other ‘it is not’, and only one can fit (dang). Bian is a practice of distinguishing (bian 辨). It asks whether a name fits a thing, and it uses analogical procedures such as ‘parallelising’ (mou) and ‘inferring’ (tui). The Mohists rejected Zhuangzi-style relativism: someone wins every genuine dispute.
methods.third_party: None required: the fit of name to thing decides.
methods.ends_well_when: One side is shown to fit (dang).
methods.typical_failure: Disputes over indexical ‘this’ and ‘that’ do not resolve by fit.

critique.text: Your ‘this’ is my ‘that’. No judge can stand outside both of us to say who fits.

methods.name: Rectification of names
methods.when: Analects (5th c. BCE); Xunzi ch. 22 (3rd c. BCE)
methods.summary: ‘If names are not correct, speech will not accord with things’ (Analects 13.3). For Xunzi, disordered names breed disordered disputes. The cure is a sage-king who fixes names by convention, after which the people need not dispute. Disagreement is diagnosed as a semantic disorder with a political remedy.
moves: Settle terminology by authority and convention
Treat clever disputation that confuses names as subversion
methods.ends_well_when: Names are settled; disputes cease.
methods.typical_failure: Semantics by decree.

critique.text: The name that can be named is not the constant name. Fixing names fixes nothing that matters.

methods.name: Walking two roads
methods.native: 兩行 liǎngxíng; 以明 yǐmíng
methods.summary: Suppose you and I argue and you beat me: does that make you right? No third party can adjudicate, since any judge either agrees with one of us or with neither. The sage stops at the pivot of the Way (daoshu), lets ‘this’ and ‘that’ both proceed, and uses the light (yiming) of seeing that each ‘this’ is someone else’s ‘that’. This is a mockery of Mohist bian that is also a technique.
moves: Stand at the hinge where both are allowed
methods.third_party: None; there is no neutral judge.
methods.ends_well_when: Both sides allowed to proceed; the sage rests at the hinge.
methods.typical_failure: Detachment that cannot act or decide.

critique.text: Zhuangzi was fixated on Heaven and did not understand the human. Society needs names and decisions.

methods.name: Court policy debate
methods.who: Han court officials vs. Confucian ‘worthies and literati’
methods.summary: An imperial conference on the state monopolies of salt and iron, written up by Huan Kuan as a set-piece dialogue. On one side stood fiscal statecraft and frontier defence. On the other stood agrarian virtue and the Confucian distrust of profit. It is an early documented instance of structured policy debate between institutional factions before a sovereign arbiter.
moves: Each faction speaks in turn before the throne
Arguments from precedent, classic and consequence
methods.third_party: The throne, which hears and decides.
methods.ends_well_when: Policy decided by the sovereign.
methods.typical_failure: The record is a partisan reworking.

critique.text: Huan Kuan wrote decades later as a sympathiser of the literati. The ‘debate’ is a literary construction.

methods.name: Dispute for the sake of Heaven
methods.native: מחלוקת לשם שמים machloket l’shem shamayim
methods.when: Hillel & Shammai 1st c. BCE; Mishnah c. 200 CE; Bavli c. 500–600
methods.summary: Avot 5:17: a dispute for the sake of Heaven will endure, and the model is Hillel and Shammai. A dispute not for Heaven’s sake will not endure, and the model is Korah. The Mishnah records the minority view (Eduyot 1:5) so that a later court may rely on it. In Eruvin 13b a heavenly voice declares ‘these and these are the words of the living God’, yet the law follows Hillel, because his school was gentle and taught Shammai’s view first. In the oven of Akhnai (Bava Metzia 59b) the majority overrules a heavenly voice: ‘it is not in heaven’.
moves: Decide by majority without declaring the minority false
Judge the dispute by its motive, not its outcome
State the opponent’s view before your own
methods.third_party: The court and the majority, which decide practice without erasing the minority.
methods.ends_well_when: A ruling for practice; all views preserved for study.
methods.typical_failure: Dispute for victory masquerading as dispute for Heaven (Korah).

critique.who: Sanhedrin 88b; Maimonides, Introduction to the Mishnah Commentary
critique.text: Disputes multiplied when students did not serve their teachers enough. Disagreement records a loss of transmitted knowledge.

methods.name: Havruta
methods.summary: Two learners argue their way through a text aloud. ‘As iron sharpens iron, so two scholars sharpen one another’ (Taanit 7a). ‘Either companionship or death’ (Taanit 23a). Holzer and Kent analyse it as three paired practices: listening and articulating, wondering and focusing, supporting and challenging. The disagreement is aimed at the text more than at the partner.
methods.third_party: The text, and behind it the teacher.
methods.ends_well_when: A reading both partners can defend.
methods.typical_failure: Cleverness for its own sake (pilpul).

critique.text: Hair-splitting dialectic trains ingenuity, not understanding, and distorts the plain sense of the law.

methods.name: Jadal & munāẓara
methods.who: Jurists and theologians; Ibn ʿAqīl; Shams al-Dīn al-Samarqandī
methods.summary: Juridical dialectic (jadal) structured legal reasoning in the madrasa through question and objection. Samarqandī’s ‘etiquette of inquiry and disputation’ later recast it as a general theory with fixed roles: claimant, questioner, and the permitted objections (manʿ, naqḍ, muʿāraḍa). The famous majlis of 932 between al-Sīrāfī and Abū Bishr Mattā was itself a dispute about what disputes are about: universal logic, or the grammar of a particular language.
moves: Claimant asserts; questioner may demand proof (manʿ)
methods.third_party: The patron’s majlis or the madrasa audience.
methods.ends_well_when: The claimant’s proof stands or falls under the permitted objections.
methods.typical_failure: Display, envy and rivalry.

critique.who: al-Ghazālī, Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn, Book of Knowledge
critique.text: Disputation for display breeds envy, pride and hatred, the vices it claims to tame.

methods.name: Science of juristic disagreement
methods.summary: Juristic disagreement is catalogued and explained rather than eliminated. The hadith of ijtihād holds that a judge who strives and is right earns two rewards, and one who strives and errs still earns one. Ibn Rushd’s handbook traces each disagreement to its cause: an ambiguous term, conflicting reports, an analogy pulling against a text. The genre is in effect an ancient account of the burdens of judgment.
moves: Diagnose the source (sabab) of the difference
methods.ends_well_when: The disagreement is explained, not ended.
methods.typical_failure: Legitimised plurality becomes cover for arbitrary choice.

critique.text: Truth in God’s law is one. Disagreement among the schools is not mercy but error to be corrected from the texts.

methods.name: Scholastic disputation
methods.who: Abelard; Aquinas; the Paris and Oxford faculties
methods.summary: Abelard’s Sic et Non set authorities against one another, and its prologue gives rules for reconciling them: check the text, the context, and above all the senses of words. The university disputation institutionalised this. The opponens objects, the respondens answers, and the master determines. Every article of the Summa keeps the trace: objections (videtur quod), counter-authority (sed contra), response (respondeo), and replies, often by distinguo.
moves: Determine; then answer each objection, typically by distinction
methods.ends_well_when: A determination that answers every objection.
methods.typical_failure: Endless distinctions; questions nobody needs answered.

critique.text: The theologians fence themselves with definitions, conclusions and corollaries, and are puffed up by their subtlety.

methods.name: Obligational disputation
methods.who: Walter Burley; Roger Swyneshed; William of Ockham
methods.summary: A formal logic game. The respondent is ‘obliged’ to maintain a possibly false proposition (the positum). The opponent then proposes further sentences, which the respondent must grant, deny or doubt so as to keep the set consistent. The respondent loses by contradiction. It is commitment management, and modern scholars read it as an ancestor of belief-revision and dialogue logics.
moves: Grant what follows; deny what is incompatible; answer irrelevant sentences by their truth
methods.third_party: A master who sets the positum.
methods.ends_well_when: The respondent survives the time limit without contradiction.
methods.typical_failure: A game cut off from any real question.

critique.text: These sophistical exercises teach young men to talk nonsense with technical precision.

methods.name: Staged religious disputation
methods.summary: Before a king, Jewish scholars were compelled to debate Christian (often convert) disputants on whether the Talmud attests the Messiah’s advent. The outcome was politically fixed before it began. Nahmanides was granted freedom of speech and was later prosecuted for publishing his account. The form of disputation persisted while its content became theatre of domination.
moves: Sovereign sets the question and the limits of speech
Victory declared by the stronger party
methods.third_party: The sovereign, who sets terms and declares the winner.
methods.ends_well_when: Victory declared by power.
methods.typical_failure: It is not a disputation at all.

critique.text: Speech under a king’s licence, before a hostile court, decides nothing; the speaker pays for winning.

methods.name: Free conversation
methods.summary: Montaigne calls conversation ‘the most fruitful and natural exercise of our mind’. He welcomes contradiction: ‘when someone opposes me, he arouses my attention, not my anger’. What he hates is obstinacy and the scholastic manner that cares more for forms than for truth. Disagreement is pleasurable friction between well-made minds, a model taken up by the salon and the honnête homme.
moves: Prefer order and liveliness to form
methods.ends_well_when: Both minds exercised; pleasure in the encounter.
methods.typical_failure: Ease without conclusion; a gentleman’s game.

critique.who: Pascal, Entretien avec M. de Sacy (1655)
critique.text: Montaigne’s easy doubt rests comfortably on a pillow of ignorance. It never faces the question that matters.

methods.name: Experimental matter of fact
methods.summary: After civil war over doctrine, natural philosophers moved dispute off contested causes and onto witnessed matters of fact. These were produced by machines such as the air-pump, attested by gentlemen, and reported in a modest style. Shapin and Schaffer show this was as much a political technology as an epistemic one: a way of making disagreement safe by giving it a narrow, public, inspectable object. Hobbes saw it as a recipe for faction.
moves: Narrow the dispute to an observable
Separate fact from hypothesis; tolerate disagreement about the latter
methods.ends_well_when: An attested matter of fact.
methods.typical_failure: Facts are made by instruments and witnesses that can themselves be disputed.

critique.text: An experimental society is a new faction. Its ‘facts’ are opinions of a closed club, and the air-pump leaks.

methods.name: Free and open encounter
methods.summary: Milton wrote: ‘Let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?’ Mill’s second chapter gives the argument its canonical form. The suppressed opinion may be true. It may hold part of the truth. Even if false, its collision with truth keeps truth from becoming dead dogma. ‘He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.’
moves: Seek the strongest form of the opposing view
Treat orthodoxy as needing periodic re-defence
methods.ends_well_when: Truth emerges or is re-earned through collision.
methods.typical_failure: The loudest voices dominate the ‘marketplace’.

critique.text: Formal tolerance under unequal power reproduces the established order. Neutral discussion favours the side already winning.

methods.name: Coffeehouse & public sphere
methods.who: London coffeehouses; Parisian salons; German Tischgesellschaften
methods.summary: On Habermas’s account, private people came together as a public to argue about matters of common concern. Status was bracketed, at least in principle, and only the argument counted. The penny university and the periodical press formed one circuit. Critics note how much was excluded, but the ideal of rational-critical debate among equals sets the norm for later deliberative theory.
moves: Argue in public about common concerns
methods.ends_well_when: Public opinion formed by argument.
methods.typical_failure: Bracketing of status leaves status intact.

critique.text: The bourgeois public sphere was built on exclusions of women, workers and others, who formed counter-publics of their own.

methods.name: Calculemus
methods.summary: Leibniz imagined a universal characteristic in which reasoning would be calculation. ‘When there are disputes among persons, we can simply say: let us calculate, without further ado, to see who is right.’ Disagreement would become an arithmetic error, detectable on paper. The dream has never been realised and has never died. It lives on in decision theory, Bayesian epistemology and the double crux.
methods.ends_well_when: A computation shows who is right.
methods.typical_failure: Most disputes do not formalise.

critique.who: Thomas Kuhn, Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)
critique.text: There is no neutral algorithm for theory choice. Even scientists cannot calculate their way across a paradigm.

methods.name: Sovereign arbitration
methods.summary: Since no one’s reason is ‘right reason’ by nature, ‘the parties must by their own accord set up for right reason the reason of some arbitrator or judge’. Without this, dispute degenerates toward war. This is the purest form of a procedural answer: do not resolve the disagreement, transfer its outcome to an authority both sides have pre-committed to obey.
moves: Accept the determination as if it were right reason
methods.ends_well_when: The arbiter’s sentence, accepted as if right reason.
methods.typical_failure: The arbiter becomes the most dangerous party.

critique.text: Men take care to avoid harm from polecats or foxes, but are content to be devoured by lions.

methods.name: Adversarial trial & cross-examination
methods.when: lawyerisation of English criminal trial from the 1730s
methods.summary: Truth is to emerge from a contest between partisan advocates before a passive judge and lay jury. Wigmore called cross-examination ‘beyond any doubt the greatest legal engine ever invented for the discovery of truth’. Langbein traces how defence counsel entered English felony trials only in the 1730s, and with them the modern theory that partisanship itself is truth-conducive.
moves: Each side presents its own case
Test the other’s witnesses by cross-examination
methods.ends_well_when: A verdict.
methods.typical_failure: The better-funded advocate wins.

critique.text: The ‘fight theory’ of justice obstructs the ‘truth theory’. Partisan coaching distorts testimony.

methods.name: Parliamentary debate
methods.when: Bill of Rights 1689; codified by Jefferson 1801, May 1844, Robert 1876
methods.who: Westminster; US Congress; Henry M. Robert
methods.summary: Rule-governed adversarial deliberation that ends in a division. Motions, amendments, speaking in turn and through the chair, and the ban on imputing motives to members all contain hostility without denying it. The ‘loyal opposition’ (Hobhouse, 1826) formalises disagreement as a permanent and legitimate office. Rules of order are a technology for making a body decide while still divided.
moves: Address the chair, not the opponent
methods.third_party: The Speaker or chair, who keeps order but does not decide.
methods.ends_well_when: A division; the majority prevails.
methods.typical_failure: Debate as theatre; decisions made elsewhere.

critique.who: Carl Schmitt, The Crisis of Parliamentary Democracy (1923)
critique.text: Public discussion has become an empty formality. Real decisions are made by parties and interests behind closed doors.

methods.name: Competitive debate
methods.when: London debating societies 1770s; Cambridge Union 1815; Oxford Union 1823; Lincoln–Douglas 1858
methods.who: Debating societies; school and university leagues
methods.summary: Sides are assigned, often by lot, and the speaker argues whatever they are given. Ticketed London debating societies of the 1770s–90s took up questions of politics, religion and the sexes. The Unions trained a governing class. The modern tournament formats (British Parliamentary, policy, Lincoln–Douglas) descend from in utramque partem. They prize advocacy over belief, which is either their virtue or their vice.
moves: Adjudicated by judges or audience vote
methods.ends_well_when: A winner on points.
methods.typical_failure: Training in advocacy without conviction.

critique.text: Treating every issue as a two-sided fight polarises and hides the many-sidedness of real questions.

methods.name: Sense of the meeting
methods.summary: No vote is taken. The clerk listens for and minutes the ‘sense of the meeting’, the unity the gathered body discerns under divine guidance. A Friend who disagrees may ‘stand aside’ or may block. Disagreement is read as unfinished discernment, not as opposing interests, and silence is a working instrument. This is the source of most secular consensus process.
moves: Each speaks once, to the meeting not to each other
Clerk proposes a minute; stand aside or stand in the way
methods.third_party: The clerk, who discerns and minutes the sense of the meeting.
methods.ends_well_when: Unity, or a recorded stand-aside.
methods.typical_failure: Fails when interests genuinely conflict or shared faith is absent.

critique.text: Unitary, consensual democracy works where interests are common. Where they conflict, it hides the conflict and favours the articulate.

methods.name: Palaver & consensus
methods.who: Akan (Asante) councils; West African palaver traditions
methods.summary: Wiredu reconstructs Asante council politics as consensual rather than majoritarian. Talk continues until a position is reached that all can accept as a basis for action, though not necessarily one all believe true. The premise is that ultimate interests are shared even when immediate interests conflict. Wiredu offers it as a model for a ‘non-party polity’.
moves: Talk until a common basis for action is found
Separate agreement on action from agreement on belief
methods.ends_well_when: A shared basis for action.
methods.typical_failure: Consensus that silences juniors, women and outsiders.

critique.text: Appeals to traditional consensus can mask hierarchy and supply cover for one-party rule.

methods.name: Activist consensus process
methods.when: Movement for a New Society 1971; anti-nuclear and Occupy movements
methods.who: Movement for a New Society; Clamshell Alliance; Occupy
methods.summary: Quaker practice secularised for movements. It uses facilitator roles, temperature checks, blocks and stand-asides. Disagreement is treated as information about a proposal’s weakness. Its known pathologies are tyranny of the patient, exhaustion and the hidden veto. These inspired later hybrids (sociocracy’s ‘consent’, ‘no paramount objection’).
moves: Test for consensus; record stand-asides; honour blocks
methods.ends_well_when: No remaining block.
methods.typical_failure: Hidden elites and exhaustion; the patient minority rules.

critique.text: Groups without formal structure develop informal elites who are unaccountable because invisible.

methods.name: Speculative dialectic
methods.summary: Each shape of consciousness, pressed to its own standard, generates its contradiction and is sublated: cancelled, preserved and raised. Disagreement is the motor of thought and of history. The textbook formula ‘thesis–antithesis–synthesis’ is Fichte’s and Chalybäus’s, not Hegel’s (Mueller 1958). The master–servant section makes the struggle for recognition the primal scene of conflict.
moves: Take the position at its word
Determine the richer standpoint that contains both
methods.third_party: None; the movement of the concept itself.
methods.ends_well_when: Sublation into a richer standpoint.
methods.typical_failure: Every opponent is pre-absorbed into the system.

critique.text: A system of existence cannot be given. The existing individual and their decision fall outside every mediation.

methods.name: Eristic dialectic
methods.summary: Schopenhauer gives thirty-eight stratagems ‘for being right’, with the opponent’s ruin as the explicit aim. The diagnosis is moral psychology. If people were honest, every debate would aim at truth. But innate vanity cannot bear to be wrong, so in most cases we argue for victory. The final stratagem, when all else fails, is to become personal.
moves: Extend the opponent’s claim beyond its limits
methods.ends_well_when: Victory, by whatever stratagem works.
methods.typical_failure: It works, which is the problem.

critique.who: Anatol Rapoport, Fights, Games, and Debates (1960)
critique.text: Stratagems raise the opponent’s sense of threat and make them less able to hear. Victory in a debate persuades no one.

methods.name: Community of inquiry
methods.summary: Doubt is an irritation that inquiry relieves. Peirce ranks four ways of fixing belief: tenacity, authority, the a priori method, and science. Only science lets ‘some external permanency’ settle opinion, so that all who investigate will in the long run converge. Disagreement is a temporary state of an unfinished inquiry, and the remedy is more and better-designed inquiry.
moves: Convert dispute into a question with an investigable answer
Defer final verdict to the community in the long run
methods.third_party: Reality, through the community of investigators.
methods.ends_well_when: Convergence in the long run.
methods.typical_failure: ‘The long run’ may never come for this dispute.

critique.text: Nothing guarantees convergence. ‘What inquiry would end in’ adds nothing to ‘what we now justify’.

methods.name: Integration
methods.summary: Conflict is ‘the appearance of difference, difference of opinions, of interests’, and should be used rather than deplored. There are three ways to deal with it. Domination gives one side its way. Compromise makes each side give up something. Integration finds a solution in which ‘both desires have found a place’. In her library example, one reader wanted the window open and another wanted it shut, and opening a window in the next room satisfied both. Getting to Yes is largely Follett with case studies.
moves: Bring the difference into the open
Break each demand into its constituent desires
Invent an option that satisfies both
methods.ends_well_when: An integration in which both desires find a place.
methods.typical_failure: Not every conflict can be integrated.

critique.text: Some conflicts are antagonistic. Treating them as integrable differences makes the stronger party’s frame the default.

methods.name: Strategic bargaining
methods.who: John Nash; Thomas Schelling; Howard Raiffa
methods.summary: Conflict is a mixed-motive game: the parties share an interest in agreement and differ on its terms. Nash derives a unique bargaining solution from axioms. Schelling shows that commitment, focal points and threats shape outcomes more than arguments do. Raiffa turns this into practical analysis of BATNAs and zones of possible agreement. Disagreement is modelled as payoff structure, not belief.
methods.third_party: None, or an arbitrator in some models.
methods.ends_well_when: An equilibrium agreement inside the zone of possible agreement.
methods.typical_failure: Values and identities do not show up as payoffs.

critique.who: Anatol Rapoport, Fights, Games, and Debates (1960)
critique.text: Game theory models only one kind of conflict. Debates, where the aim is to change the other’s mind, fall outside it.

methods.name: Interactive problem-solving workshop
methods.who: John Burton; Herbert Kelman; John Paul Lederach
methods.summary: Unofficial representatives of warring communities meet with a panel of social scientists. They analyse the conflict jointly instead of negotiating positions. Burton’s premise, later his human-needs theory, is that deep-rooted conflict stems from non-negotiable needs for identity, security and recognition. These needs, unlike interests, cannot be bargained away and must be satisfied. Lederach widened this into ‘conflict transformation’ of relationships and structures.
moves: Third party as facilitator, not judge
Surface needs and fears; co-design options
methods.third_party: A panel of scholar-practitioners as facilitators.
methods.ends_well_when: Shared analysis and new options carried back home.
methods.typical_failure: Insights do not transfer to official negotiators.

critique.who: Evaluators of track-two diplomacy (‘the transfer problem’)
critique.text: Changed minds in a workshop rarely change policy. Power sits with people who were not in the room.

methods.name: Restorative justice & circles
methods.who: Howard Zehr; John Braithwaite; Kay Pranis
methods.summary: Crime and conflict are reframed as harm to people and relationships, not violation of a rule against the state. Victim, offender and community meet in a facilitated encounter or a talking-piece circle to name the harm, take responsibility and repair. Braithwaite adds ‘reintegrative shaming’: disapproval of the act within continued respect for the person.
moves: Who was harmed? What do they need? Whose obligation?
methods.ends_well_when: Agreement on repair; relationship restored.
methods.typical_failure: Pressure on victims to forgive.

critique.text: The promise of healing and reconciliation can coerce victims and sentimentalise justice.

methods.name: Mediation
methods.when: Pound Conference 1976; Bush & Folger 1994; Winslade & Monk 2000
methods.who: Frank Sander; Robert Baruch Bush & Joseph Folger; John Winslade & Gerald Monk
methods.summary: Sander’s ‘multi-door courthouse’ launched modern alternative dispute resolution: send each dispute to the process that fits it. Facilitative mediation seeks interest-based settlement. Transformative mediation drops settlement as the goal and aims at empowerment and recognition, so that each party regains clarity and sees the other. Narrative mediation, drawing on Foucault, helps parties deconstruct ‘conflict-saturated stories’ and co-author alternatives.
moves: Neutral third party controls process, not outcome
Follow the parties’ shifts in empowerment and recognition (transformative)
methods.third_party: A neutral mediator who controls process, not outcome.
methods.ends_well_when: A voluntary agreement; or, in transformative mode, empowerment and recognition.
methods.typical_failure: Private settlement under power imbalance.

critique.text: Settlement trades justice for peace. Power imbalances go unremedied and public norms go unmade.

methods.name: Principled negotiation
methods.summary: The method has four rules. Separate the people from the problem. Focus on interests, not positions. Invent options for mutual gain. Insist on objective criteria. Know your BATNA. The epistemic core is the claim that positions are lossy encodings of interests, and that interests are more often compatible than positions are.
moves: Agree on standards before applying them
methods.ends_well_when: A wise agreement measured by objective criteria.
methods.typical_failure: Ignores the hard distributive core.

critique.who: James J. White, review of Getting to Yes (1984)
critique.text: Most negotiation is distributive. Fisher and Ury wish away the part where one side’s gain is the other’s loss.

methods.name: Difficult conversations
methods.who: Douglas Stone; Bruce Patton; Sheila Heen
methods.summary: Every hard conversation is three conversations at once. The ‘what happened’ conversation is about truth, intent and blame. The feelings conversation is about what each person feels. The identity conversation asks what this says about me: am I competent, good, lovable? Shift from certainty to curiosity, from blame to contribution, from inferred intent to reported impact.
moves: Map joint contribution instead of blame
methods.ends_well_when: Each person understands the three conversations; a way forward.
methods.typical_failure: Treats structural conflict as interpersonal.

critique.text: Reframing conflict as perception and identity can personalise what is really about position and resources.

methods.name: Rogerian exchange
methods.summary: Rogers names ‘our very natural tendency to judge, to evaluate’ as the main barrier to communication. His test is that each person may speak up for himself only after he has first restated the ideas and feelings of the previous speaker accurately, and to that speaker’s satisfaction. Rhetoricians turned this into ‘Rogerian argument’: reduce threat, state the opponent’s position fairly, find common ground, then propose.
moves: Restate the other’s view to their satisfaction before replying
methods.third_party: None; or a facilitator enforcing the rule.
methods.ends_well_when: Each side understood to its satisfaction.
methods.typical_failure: Asks the weaker party to accommodate.

critique.who: Phyllis Lassner, ‘Feminist Responses to Rogerian Argument’ (1990)
critique.text: For those already expected to accommodate, the Rogerian demand to suppress judgment repeats their silencing.

methods.name: Rapoport’s rules & region of validity
methods.summary: Rapoport distinguishes three kinds of conflict. In fights the aim is to harm the opponent. In games the aim is to outwit them within rules. In debates the aim is to convince them. In a true debate one must reduce the opponent’s sense of threat by showing that one understands their position. One does this by stating the ‘region of validity’ in which their view is correct. Dennett distilled this into four rules: re-express, list agreements, mention what you learned, and only then rebut.
moves: Re-express their position so well they wish they had said it
methods.ends_well_when: The opponent feels understood and can hear the rebuttal.
methods.typical_failure: Useless against someone fighting, not debating.

critique.text: When the aim is to harm, not to convince, no technique of debate applies.

methods.name: Nonviolent Communication
methods.summary: Every utterance can be heard as an expression of observation, feeling, need and request. Judgments, demands and diagnoses are ‘tragic expressions of unmet needs’. Needs are universal and never actually in conflict. Strategies are what collide. Disagreement is thus re-described at the level where, by hypothesis, it disappears.
methods.ends_well_when: Needs named and a request accepted.
methods.typical_failure: Scripted empathy; jargon used as a weapon.

critique.text: Recasting injustice as unmet need can depoliticise grievances and leave power untouched.

methods.name: Motivational interviewing
methods.summary: Arguing for change produces resistance, because the listener voices the other side of their own ambivalence. MI instead uses reflective listening to evoke the person’s own reasons for change, and it ‘rolls with resistance’. It is a clinical method that has become a general template for persuasion without confrontation, and it is a direct ancestor of street epistemology and deep canvassing.
methods.ends_well_when: The person voices their own reasons for change.
methods.typical_failure: Steering dressed as neutrality.

critique.text: A technique that evokes change by design must guard against manipulating autonomy it claims to respect.

methods.name: Bohmian dialogue
methods.summary: A group of about twenty to forty people meets without agenda or decision. Participants practise suspending their assumptions, neither acting on them nor suppressing them, so that the group can observe thought as a collective, self-sustaining process. Disagreement shows where unexamined assumptions defend themselves as if they were the self.
moves: No agenda, no leader, no decision
Attend to the flow of meaning between participants
methods.third_party: Facilitator only at first; then none.
methods.ends_well_when: Shared meaning; thought seen as a collective process.
methods.typical_failure: Endless talk without decision.

critique.text: Groups with real stakes cannot suspend forever. Some decisions must be made by people with conflicting interests.

methods.name: Reflective structured dialogue
methods.who: Laura Chasin; Richard Chasin; Margaret Herzig
methods.summary: Family therapists applied systemic techniques to polarised public issues, starting with abortion. Participants agree to communication rules. They answer prepared questions in timed rounds, beginning with personal experience. They are asked to name uncertainties and ‘grey areas’ within their own view. The aim is to break the ‘old conversation’ of stereotyped positions and to make each side’s complexity visible.
methods.ends_well_when: Stereotypes broken; complexity visible.
methods.typical_failure: Civility without change.

critique.text: Dialogue that lowers the temperature can depoliticise conflicts that need to be fought out.

methods.name: Street epistemology
methods.summary: This is the elenchus crossed with motivational interviewing. The questioner targets not the belief but the method by which the belief is held, asks for a confidence level, and explores what would change it. It is openly persuasive in intent, though practitioners stress rapport and the interlocutor’s autonomy.
moves: Identify a claim and a confidence level
methods.ends_well_when: The interlocutor lowers their confidence or examines their method.
methods.typical_failure: Persuasion disguised as inquiry.

critique.text: If you already know where you want the other to end up, the questions are a technique, not an inquiry.

methods.name: Moral reframing
methods.summary: People argue in the moral foundations of their own side, and so fail to persuade the other. Experiments find that framing a position in the opponent’s moral terms, such as environmentalism framed as purity or a liberal policy framed as patriotism, measurably increases support. This is Aristotle’s audience-adaptation with a psychometric instrument.
methods.ends_well_when: Measurable increase in support.
methods.typical_failure: Instrumentalises the other’s values.

critique.text: Arguing in values you do not hold is a kind of insincerity, and audiences can tell.

methods.name: Deep canvassing
methods.who: Leadership LAB (Los Angeles LGBT Center); David Broockman; Joshua Kalla
methods.summary: Canvassers hold ten-minute door-step conversations. They ask for the voter’s view, listen non-judgmentally, exchange personal stories, and invite the voter to reflect on a time they were judged. Field experiments found durable attitude change. An earlier, fabricated study of the method (LaCour & Green, 2014, retracted 2015) makes the later replication more, not less, significant.
methods.ends_well_when: Measurable, durable attitude change.
methods.typical_failure: Effects smaller and less general than hoped.

critique.text: Effects vary by issue and context. The early retracted study inflated expectations.

methods.name: Toulmin model
methods.summary: Practical argument is modelled jurisprudentially, not geometrically. A claim rests on data through a warrant, which has backing and is limited by a qualifier and rebuttals. Many disagreements turn out to sit at the warrant, the inference licence, and not at the data or the claim. Warrants are ‘field-dependent’, so disputes across fields need a meta-argument about which warrants govern.
moves: Locate the disagreement: data, warrant, backing or qualifier
methods.ends_well_when: The disagreement located at data, warrant or backing.
methods.typical_failure: Field-dependence leaves cross-field disputes open.

critique.text: A warrant is just a suppressed premise. Toulmin’s layout adds nothing a valid argument form lacks.

methods.name: Formal dialectic & dialogue types
methods.who: C. L. Hamblin; Douglas Walton; Erik Krabbe
methods.summary: Hamblin modelled argument as a rule-governed game in which each move updates a participant’s commitment store, and he defined fallacies as illegal moves. Walton and Krabbe classified dialogue by initial situation and goal: persuasion, inquiry, negotiation, deliberation, information-seeking and eristic. A fallacy then often turns out to be a covert shift from one dialogue type to another.
moves: Name the dialogue type in play
methods.ends_well_when: Commitments made explicit; fallacies flagged.
methods.typical_failure: Idealises away emotion and power.

critique.text: Real arguers are not commitment stores. Fear, status and identity drive the moves the model calls fallacies.

methods.name: Discourse ethics
methods.summary: Every speech act raises validity claims: truth, normative rightness, sincerity and comprehensibility. When a claim is contested, communication shifts into discourse, where only ‘the unforced force of the better argument’ should count. Norms are valid if all affected could accept them as participants in such discourse. Disagreement is a breakdown in mutual understanding that discourse is designed to repair.
moves: Identify the validity claim at issue
Accept only reasons all could share
methods.third_party: None; the ideal community of discourse.
methods.ends_well_when: Consensus under ideal conditions.
methods.typical_failure: Consensus as a hidden demand to speak in one idiom.

critique.text: Consensus is an outmoded and suspect value. It does violence to the heterogeneity of language games.

methods.name: Pragma-dialectics
methods.summary: An ideal model of ‘critical discussion’ for resolving a difference of opinion on the merits. It runs through four stages: confrontation, opening, argumentation and concluding. Ten rules govern it, among them the freedom rule, the burden-of-proof rule, the standpoint rule and the closure rule. Each fallacy is a violation of a specific rule at a specific stage. Later work on ‘strategic manoeuvring’ admits that real arguers want both to be reasonable and to win.
methods.third_party: None; an analyst may reconstruct the discussion.
methods.ends_well_when: Standpoint retracted or doubt withdrawn.
methods.typical_failure: Real arguers are not ideal discussants.

critique.who: Mercier & Sperber, The Enigma of Reason (2017)
critique.text: Reasoning evolved for persuasion and is biased in production. An ideal model must be engineered around that, not assumed away.

methods.name: Deliberative polling
methods.summary: A random sample of citizens is polled, given balanced briefing materials and competing experts, and deliberates in moderated small groups over a weekend. The sample is then polled again. The output is a counterfactual: what the public would think if it had the chance to think. Disagreement is treated as partly a product of inattention and misinformation, which deliberation reduces, and partly as real and reportable.
methods.ends_well_when: A measured, considered public opinion.
methods.typical_failure: Deliberation favours the already-fluent.

critique.text: Deliberation’s norms of reasoned speech privilege those already advantaged. Testimony may be fairer than argument.

methods.name: Agonistic pluralism
methods.summary: Against Habermasian consensus, Mouffe argues that antagonism is ineradicable and every consensus is a hegemonic settlement that excludes. The democratic task is to turn antagonism (enemy against enemy) into agonism (adversary against adversary): opponents who share allegiance to liberty and equality and fight over their interpretation. Disagreement should be given institutional channels, not dissolved.
moves: Name the conflict as political, not moral
methods.ends_well_when: None final; conflict channelled.
methods.typical_failure: No criterion separates adversary from enemy.

critique.text: Without shared standards of justification, agonism cannot say why anyone should accept defeat.

methods.name: Citizens’ assemblies
methods.who: BC Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform; Irish Citizens’ Assembly
methods.summary: A body selected by lot hears evidence, deliberates over weeks or months, and recommends. The Irish Assembly’s recommendation on the Eighth Amendment preceded the 2018 referendum. Gutmann and Thompson supply the normative frame. Moral disagreement is permanent and reasonable, so the rules of deliberation should be reciprocity, publicity and accountability, not the hope of agreement.
methods.ends_well_when: A recommendation, usually to parliament or referendum.
methods.typical_failure: A small group decides for millions.

critique.text: Assemblies are a shortcut: citizens are asked to defer to a body they did not authorise.

methods.name: Bridging systems
methods.who: Colin Megill et al. (Pol.is); Audrey Tang; X/Twitter
methods.summary: Participants vote agree or disagree on short statements written by one another. Dimensionality reduction maps the opinion clusters, and the system surfaces statements that win support across clusters. Community Notes publishes a fact-check only when raters who usually disagree both rate it helpful. Disagreement is modelled as geometry, and the target is the bridging statement, not the median.
methods.ends_well_when: Statements that win support across clusters.
methods.typical_failure: Bridging rewards blandness.

critique.text: Truths held by one cluster never surface. The bridging statement is often the vaguest one.

methods.name: AI-mediated deliberation
methods.summary: A language model drafts group statements from individual opinions, collects critiques, and revises. In UK experiments the AI-mediated statements were preferred over those of human mediators, and they reduced within-group division. This raises an old question in new form: whose ‘common ground’ does the mediator find, and what does it leave out?
methods.ends_well_when: A group statement most participants endorse.
methods.typical_failure: Whose common ground? The model’s priors shape it.

critique.text: A mediator trained by a company encodes contestable values and may homogenise dissent.

methods.name: Adversarial collaboration
methods.summary: Scientists who disagree co-design a study whose outcome each agrees in advance would count against their view. An arbiter holds the data. Kahneman proposed it as an alternative to the ‘angry science’ of comment and reply. It works best when the dispute can be operationalised, and it reveals how often it cannot.
moves: Agree on the crucial experiment in advance
methods.third_party: An arbiter who holds the data.
methods.ends_well_when: A jointly agreed result.
methods.typical_failure: Few participants actually change their minds.

critique.text: Even after agreed tests, collaborators rarely updated. Commitment to a view is also commitment to a self.

methods.name: Ideological Turing test & steelmanning
methods.summary: Can you state your opponent’s view so well that their own side cannot tell you from a true believer? Caplan’s test, taking off from Mill’s ‘know the other side’, operationalises understanding as indistinguishability. Steelmanning asks for the strongest version, which may be stronger than the one its holders actually hold. That subtle difference sometimes turns charity into ventriloquism.
moves: Have its adherents judge whether it passes
methods.ends_well_when: Indistinguishability from a true believer.
methods.typical_failure: Mimicry without understanding.

critique.text: One can learn a vocabulary well enough to pass without sharing the form of life that gives it sense.

methods.name: Double crux
methods.who: Center for Applied Rationality; Duncan Sabien
methods.summary: Each party finds their crux, a belief that, if it changed, would change their conclusion. Then they look for a double crux: a single empirical or conceptual question on which both conclusions depend in opposite directions. The dispute is moved down the belief-graph until it reaches something testable. This assumes disagreement is a matter of models and that both parties are trying to be right. Aumann’s theorem stands in the background.
moves: Find your crux: ‘if B were false, would I change my mind?’
methods.ends_well_when: A shared crux identified and investigated.
methods.typical_failure: Value and identity disputes have no crux.

critique.who: From the standpoint of value pluralism (Weber, Berlin)
critique.text: Not every disagreement bottoms out in a testable belief. Some end at incompatible goods.

views.name: Error & ignorance
views.who: Plato; Aquinas; most of the rationalist tradition
views.summary: Two contradictory claims cannot both be true, so at least one party is wrong. Disagreement is a symptom of error, and error is a privation, a lack of knowledge. Socratic intellectualism adds that no one errs willingly. Correct the belief and the dispute dissolves. This is the default account, so pervasive it is rarely stated.
views.implies: Inquiry, refutation, instruction.

quote.text: No one goes willingly toward the bad.

views.name: Inconsistency & aporia
views.summary: The disagreement that matters is within a person, among beliefs they already hold. An interlocutor is shown that their commitments cannot all stand. The external opponent is only the occasion for internal disagreement. Formal dialectic later makes this precise as a commitment store that has to stay consistent.
views.implies: Elenchus, obligational games, commitment-tracking.

views.name: Disputed reputable opinion
views.summary: Some questions belong to things that ‘admit of being otherwise’, where only probable premises are available. Reputable opinions conflict, and working through the puzzles (diaporēsai) on both sides is how one approaches first principles. Disagreement is the normal texture of practical and dialectical reasoning, not a sign that someone has blundered.
views.implies: Dialectic, rhetoric, the method of endoxa (Nicomachean Ethics VII.1).

quote.text: For those who wish to get clear of difficulties it is advantageous to discuss the difficulties well.

views.name: Partial perspectives
views.who: Protagoras; Jain logicians; J. S. Mill; Nietzsche
views.summary: Each party sees a real aspect of something larger. The blind men are each right about the elephant and wrong only in saying ‘only’. Mill’s secular version holds that conflicting doctrines ‘share the truth between them’. Nietzsche’s holds that ‘there is only a perspective seeing’, and that the more eyes we bring to a thing, the more complete our ‘objectivity’.
views.implies: Standpoint indexing, both-sides argument, synthesis.

quote.text: There is only a perspective seeing, only a perspective ‘knowing’.

views.name: Undecidability
views.summary: Some disputes are interminable because the arguments on each side are of equal force (isostheneia). For Sextus this is a reason to suspend judgment. For Kant, the antinomies show reason in conflict with itself whenever it overreaches experience. The dispute is a structural feature of the question, not a fault of the disputants.
views.implies: Suspension; critique of the question; demarcation.

views.name: Calculation error
views.summary: With an adequate notation, every dispute would be a mistake in calculation, checkable like a sum. Disagreement is an artefact of natural language’s imprecision.
views.implies: Formalisation; ‘Calculemus!’

quote.text: Let us calculate, without further ado, to see who is right.

views.name: Unfinished inquiry
views.summary: Disagreement is the state of a community whose inquiry has not yet converged. Under the method of science, the opinion ‘fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate’ is what we mean by truth. Disagreement is therefore temporal, not permanent.
views.implies: Better experiments; patience; fallibilism.

views.name: Burdens of judgment
views.summary: Reasonable people disagree without any of them being irrational or ill-willed. Evidence is complex and conflicting. People weigh considerations differently. Concepts are vague at the edges. Total life experience shapes judgment. Normative considerations pull both ways, and every institution must select among values. Reasonable pluralism is the natural outcome of free reason, not a disaster.
views.implies: Toleration; public reason; deliberation without expectation of convergence.

views.name: Divergent priors & models
views.who: Robert Aumann; Robin Hanson; Tyler Cowen; CFAR
views.summary: Bayesian agents with common priors whose posteriors are common knowledge cannot agree to disagree. Persistent disagreement therefore implies different priors, private information that has not been shared, or something other than honest truth-seeking. Cowen and Hanson draw the uncomfortable conclusion that most disagreements are not honest, because each party gives its own judgment more weight than it should. The practical version breaks the dispute down into world-models and finds the crux.
views.implies: Share evidence; locate cruxes; bet; update.

views.name: Higher-order evidence
views.who: Thomas Kelly; David Christensen; Adam Elga
views.summary: Suppose you learn that an epistemic peer, someone as informed and as able as you, disagrees. Should you move toward their view? Conciliationists (Christensen, Elga) say yes: ‘equal weight’. Steadfast views (Kelly) say the first-order evidence still counts. Here disagreement is itself evidence, and evidence about one’s own reliability.
views.implies: Calibrated humility; or principled steadfastness.

views.name: Incommensurable paradigms
views.summary: Across a revolution, scientists ‘practice their trades in different worlds’. They disagree about which problems matter, what counts as a solution and what terms mean, so that there is no neutral algorithm of choice. Persuasion across paradigms resembles conversion.
views.implies: Translation, exemplars, time; not a crucial experiment.

views.name: Disorder of names
views.summary: Disputes arise when names no longer track realities and roles. For the Mohists, every bian is about whether a name fits. For Xunzi, deviant sophists who ‘confuse names’ create disorder that a true king must correct.
views.implies: Rectify names, by sage convention or by disputation.

quote.text: If names are not correct, speech will not accord with things.

views.name: Equivocation & verbal dispute
views.who: Aristotle; Peter Abelard; William James; David Chalmers
views.summary: The parties use one word in two senses and so do not really contradict each other. Aristotle classes homonymy first among the fallacies dependent on language. Abelard reconciles authorities by distinguishing senses. In James’s squirrel case, whether a man ‘goes round’ a squirrel depends on what ‘round’ means. Chalmers proposes the ‘method of elimination’: ban the contested word and see whether a dispute remains.
views.implies: Distinguo; taboo the word; restate without the term.

views.name: Disagreement in attitude
views.summary: Stevenson distinguishes disagreement in belief, about how things are, from disagreement in attitude, about what to favour. Ethical disputes are chiefly the latter, carried on in language that sounds descriptive. Belief-change can shift attitude, but nothing guarantees it will.
views.implies: Separate belief from attitude; persuasive definitions are moves, not findings.

views.name: Metalinguistic negotiation
views.summary: Many apparently factual disputes, such as whether Secretariat is an ‘athlete’ or whether waterboarding is ‘torture’, are disputes about how a word ought to be used. These disputes are real and important because words have practical consequences. A verbal dispute is not therefore a merely verbal one.
views.implies: Make the normative question about usage explicit (conceptual engineering).

views.name: Hinges & language-games
views.summary: Some propositions are not conclusions but hinges on which doubting turns. When two parties’ hinges differ, reasons run out. ‘Where two principles really do meet which cannot be reconciled with one another, then each man declares the other a fool and heretic.’ ‘At the end of reasons comes persuasion.’
views.implies: Show rather than prove; conversion; patient description of the other’s game.

views.name: Clash of final vocabularies
views.summary: Everyone carries a ‘final vocabulary’, words beyond which they have only circular argument. Disputes between vocabularies are not settled by evidence. One vocabulary is redescribed in terms of another, or the conversation simply continues. Edifying philosophy aims to keep the conversation going, not to end it with truth.
views.implies: Redescription; irony; keep the conversation going.

views.name: The differend
views.summary: A differend is a conflict between parties that cannot be equitably resolved because no rule of judgment applies to both. To settle it in one party’s idiom wrongs the other, whose harm cannot be stated in that idiom. Litigation presupposes a shared genre; a differend is precisely where none exists.
views.implies: Bear witness; find idioms for what cannot yet be phrased.

views.name: Contested validity claims
views.summary: Speech acts implicitly claim truth, rightness and sincerity. Disagreement occurs when a hearer rejects one of these claims, which tells us which kind of argument the disagreement requires: theoretical discourse, practical discourse, or the test of consistent conduct over time.
views.implies: Discourse; ideal speech situation.

views.name: What cannot be measured
views.summary: Socrates observes that disputes about number, size and weight are ended by counting, measuring and weighing. The disputes that cause anger and enmity concern the just and unjust, the noble and shameful, the good and bad, for which we have no agreed standard of decision. It is the earliest explicit statement that value disagreements differ in kind.
views.implies: Find a measure, or accept enduring enmity.

views.name: Value pluralism
views.summary: The ultimate values of life are irreconcilable. ‘The various value spheres of the world stand in irreconcilable conflict with each other.’ Berlin adds that goods are many, cannot be measured on one scale, and conflict, so that tragic loss is built into choice. Disagreement may be neither error nor confusion, but the correct perception of real incompatibility.
views.implies: Choose and own the choice; build institutions for coexistence.

quote.text: Many old gods ascend from their graves… and resume their eternal struggle with one another.

views.name: Moral foundations
views.summary: Moral judgment rests on a few intuitive foundations: care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and, later, liberty. Political camps weight these differently. Reasoning mostly follows intuition, like a rider on an elephant, so disputes conducted in one camp’s foundations do not land in the other’s.
views.implies: Moral reframing; humility about one’s own foundations.

views.name: Sacred values
views.who: Philip Tetlock; Scott Atran; Robert Axelrod
views.summary: Some values are protected from trade-offs, and offering money for them provokes moral outrage, not interest. Rational-choice bargaining backfires here. Symbolic gestures such as apology or recognition can open paths that material concessions close. Much ‘interest’ conflict is sacred-value conflict misdiagnosed.
views.implies: Symbolic concessions; reframing; never price the sacred.

views.name: Interests beneath positions
views.who: Mary Parker Follett; Roger Fisher; William Ury
views.summary: What people say they want, their positions, is a strategy for what they need, their interests. Positions are often incompatible where the interests behind them are not. Disagreement is about allocation, and allocation is a design problem.
views.implies: Ask why; invent options; integrative bargaining.

views.name: Faction & party
views.summary: Hume sorts real factions into those from interest, those from principle (‘abstract speculative principle’, which he finds peculiar to modern times) and those from affection. Madison: the ‘latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man’, and ‘the most common and durable source’ is the unequal distribution of property. These causes cannot be removed, so their effects must be controlled by an extended republic.
views.implies: Institutional design that multiplies and balances factions.

views.name: Mixed-motive game
views.summary: Conflict is rarely pure. The parties have a common interest in avoiding mutual loss and a conflicting interest over how to divide gains. What looks like argument is often signalling, commitment and the search for a focal point.
views.implies: Bargaining analysis; credible commitments; focal points.

views.name: Class interest & ideology
views.summary: ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.’ Ideas follow material positions, and the ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class. Many intellectual disagreements are class antagonisms that do not recognise themselves as such.
views.implies: Ideology critique; organising; changing the material base.

views.name: Contest & honour
views.who: Greek agonistic culture; the sophists; Schopenhauer
views.summary: Argument is a form of combat whose stake is standing. The contest is good in itself as an arena of excellence (Hesiod’s ‘good Eris’). In its degenerate form it is vanity defended by any means. What is at issue is not the proposition but who prevails before an audience.
views.implies: Rules, judges, audiences; or withdrawal from the arena.

views.name: War & sovereignty
views.summary: Private judgment about right and wrong is the seed of civil war. Dispute is a pre-political condition that only a sovereign arbiter can end. ‘Right reason’ is whatever reason the parties have agreed to treat as authoritative.
views.implies: Arbitration; delegation of judgment.

views.name: Friend & enemy
views.summary: The specifically political distinction is between friend and enemy. Any opposition, whether religious, moral or economic, becomes political when it is intense enough to group people as friends and enemies. Liberal discussion hopes to dissolve the political into endless conversation and therefore misunderstands it.
views.implies: Decision, not debate (Schmitt); or agonistic taming (Mouffe).

views.name: Hegemony
views.summary: Every social order is a contingent hegemonic articulation, and every consensus excludes. Disagreement is the trace of what the current settlement suppresses. The goal is to legitimise it, not dissolve it.
views.implies: Agonistic institutions; counter-hegemonic struggle.

views.name: Power / knowledge
views.summary: Each society has its ‘regime of truth’, which governs the types of discourse it accepts as true and who is authorised to say what counts. Disputes over truth are also struggles over the rules that produce truth. Who may speak is decided before what is said.
views.implies: Genealogy; problematisation; attention to who is authorised to speak.

views.name: Vanity & obstinacy
views.who: Schopenhauer; Montaigne; the Buddha of Sn 4
views.summary: Most people cannot bear to be shown wrong. Once a position is stated, defending it becomes a matter of self-regard, and the original question is abandoned. Montaigne thought obstinacy and heat of opinion the surest sign of a weak mind.
views.implies: Lower the stakes of being wrong; or exploit them (eristic).

views.name: Unmet needs
views.summary: Beneath interests lie universal human needs: security, identity, recognition, autonomy, meaning. These cannot be bargained over, but they can be satisfied, and they rarely truly conflict. Conflict is what unmet needs sound like.
views.implies: Needs-based dialogue; ‘provention’ (Burton’s coinage).

views.name: Threat & defensiveness
views.summary: A person who feels threatened cannot hear. Evaluation is experienced as threat, and threat produces rigidity. Many disagreements persist because each side’s argument raises the other’s defences. The obstacle is affective, not logical.
views.implies: Restate before rebutting; reduce threat; evoke rather than argue.

views.name: Narcissism of small differences
views.summary: Communities with adjoining territories, and those related to each other in other ways, are especially prone to feud and ridicule. Hostility is greatest between those who are nearly alike. Disagreement here does not track distance of views. It serves the group’s cohesion and its narcissism.
views.implies: Notice how close the opponent is.

views.name: Mimetic rivalry
views.summary: We desire what the model desires, so imitation makes rivals of those who are alike. As rivalry escalates, the object disappears and the rivals become doubles, each mirroring the other’s violence. Communities resolve the crisis by uniting against a scapegoat.
views.implies: Recognise the double; refuse the scapegoat.

views.name: Argumentative reasoning
views.who: Hugo Mercier; Dan Sperber; Dan Kahan
views.summary: Reasoning evolved to produce and evaluate arguments in social exchange, not to find truth alone. Individuals show myside bias when producing arguments and are better at judging others’ arguments. Groups that argue can outperform individuals. Kahan adds identity-protective cognition: numerate partisans polarise more on politicised facts, not less.
views.implies: Argue in groups with real diversity; decouple facts from identity.

views.name: Developmental form
views.summary: The same disagreement takes a different shape depending on how a person makes meaning. At a ‘self-authoring’ order, one is one’s ideology and conflict is between systems. At a ‘self-transforming’ order, one can hold one’s own system as object, so conflict becomes a sign of over-identification with a partial form. Chapman’s ‘meta-rationality’ treats the fit between frame and situation as the real question.
