views.implies: Hold your system as object; ask what each frame is for.

views.name: Identity
views.who: Henri Tajfel; John Turner; Douglas Stone
views.summary: People derive self-esteem from group membership, and intergroup comparison drives conflict even over trivial distinctions (the minimal-group paradigm). In dyads, the ‘identity conversation’ asks what being wrong would say about me. To concede the point is to lose the self.
views.implies: Decouple claim from identity; affirm before challenging.

views.name: Struggle for recognition
views.who: G. W. F. Hegel; Axel Honneth
views.summary: Self-consciousness exists only in being acknowledged, so the first conflict is a life-and-death struggle for recognition. Honneth turns this into a moral grammar of social conflict. Disrespect in love, rights and esteem drives struggles that present themselves as being about other things.
views.implies: Recognition as remedy; attend to disrespect beneath the stated grievance.

views.name: Relationship-level message
views.who: Paul Watzlawick; Janet Beavin Bavelas; Don Jackson
views.summary: Every communication has a content aspect and a relationship aspect, and the latter classifies the former. Couples argue about the dishes while negotiating dominance and care. Each party also ‘punctuates’ the sequence differently (‘I withdraw because you nag’; ‘I nag because you withdraw’), so each sees the other as the cause.
views.implies: Metacommunicate; change the pattern, not the topic.

views.name: Harm to relationship
views.who: Howard Zehr; restorative and indigenous traditions
views.summary: Conflict and crime are wounds in a web of relationships, not abstract violations. The question is not ‘who is right?’ or ‘what rule was broken?’ but ‘who was hurt, and what do they need?’
views.implies: Repair; circles; reintegration.

views.name: Character & motive
views.summary: Disagreement tests who you are. The Mishnah judges a dispute by whether it is ‘for the sake of Heaven’, and Socratic examination is examination of a life. The worth of the exchange lies in the disputants’ intention and virtue more than in its outcome.
views.implies: Purify motive; judge disputes by their spirit.

views.name: Affective polarisation
views.summary: Partisans increasingly dislike and distrust each other, often more than their policy differences warrant. Disagreement becomes a sorting of social identity, amplified by engagement-ranked media. The measurable object is not belief distance but cross-group affect.
views.implies: Bridging ranking; cross-cutting contact; de-sorting.

views.name: Attachment to views
views.summary: Suffering in dispute comes from grasping at views (diṭṭhi-upādāna), not from which view is right. Even right view held as a possession breeds conflict. The remedy is not a better position but release from positionality.
views.implies: Non-dispute; emptiness of views; suspension.

views.name: ‘This’ and ‘that’
views.summary: Every ‘this is so’ (shi) is made from a standpoint, and from the other side it is ‘that’ (bi). The Confucians and Mohists affirm what the other denies. The sage sees that ‘this’ and ‘that’ generate each other, and rests at the pivot from which both can be allowed.
views.implies: Walking two roads; illumination.

views.name: Incomplete discernment
views.summary: Truth is one and is discerned together. Persisting disagreement means the gathered meeting has not yet waited long enough for the Light. A lone objector may be right, which is why a block is honoured.
views.implies: Wait in silence; seek unity, not majority.

views.name: Plurality willed from above
views.summary: ‘These and these are the words of the living God.’ Contradictory rulings can both belong to revelation. Halakhic decision is necessary for practice, but the rejected opinion stays Torah, is studied, and may be revived. Disagreement is part of how revelation unfolds.
views.implies: Record minority views; decide without declaring falsehood.

views.name: Disagreement as mercy
views.summary: Diverse rulings reached by sincere ijtihād are each rewarded, even when mistaken. A saying attributed to the Prophet, ‘the disagreement of my community is a mercy’, is of weak attestation but culturally powerful. The schools’ plurality was understood as latitude for believers, not as scandal.
views.implies: Tolerate madhhab difference; study khilāf.

views.name: Strife as engine
views.summary: ‘War is father of all and king of all.’ ‘Justice is strife.’ Opposition is the motor of becoming. Hegel makes contradiction the self-movement of the concept, and Marx locates it in material relations. Disagreement is how history and thought advance.
views.implies: Sharpen, then sublate, the contradiction.

views.name: Collision with error
views.summary: Truth unchallenged becomes dead dogma. Even a false dissent is useful, because it forces truth to be re-earned and therefore understood. Disagreement is the immune system of belief.
views.implies: Free discussion; devil’s advocacy; protect dissent.

views.name: Conflict as sociation
views.summary: Conflict is a form of social relation, not its absence. It binds the antagonists, clarifies boundaries, and creates group cohesion. Cross-cutting conflicts can stitch a society together. A society without conflict would be a society without contact.
views.implies: Institutionalise, don’t suppress; foster cross-cutting cleavages.

views.name: Constructive difference
views.summary: Follett asks us to think of conflict as friction in an engine. It is neither good nor bad in itself; it is the appearance of difference, and difference is the raw material of invention. Integration produces something new that neither party brought.
views.implies: Integration over compromise.

glossary.def: Refutation by question and answer: the interlocutor’s own admissions are shown to contradict their thesis.
The impasse reached when every available answer has failed; for Plato, the beginning of inquiry.
The practice of setting an opposing argument against any given argument.
Argument aimed at victory rather than truth.
Reputable opinions: what is accepted by all, by most, or by the wise. The starting points of dialectic.
A ‘place’ or general pattern from which arguments on many subjects can be drawn.
A rhetorical syllogism, reasoning from probabilities and signs, often with a premise left unstated.
The point at which a dispute stands: fact, definition, quality or jurisdiction.
Equal force of opposing arguments, which in Pyrrhonism leads to suspension of judgment.
Suspension of judgment.
Tranquillity, freedom from disturbance; for the Pyrrhonist, the by-product of suspension.
Disagreement, the first of Agrippa’s five modes of sceptical argument.
Good-faith debate aimed at truth, between parties who rely on the accepted means of knowledge.
Wrangling: debate for victory that permits quibbles and sophistical rejoinders.
Cavil: refutation of the opponent without defending any thesis of one’s own.
A means of valid knowledge, such as perception, inference, comparison and testimony.
A ‘point of defeat’: a slip by which a debater loses.
An unwanted consequence drawn from the opponent’s own position; reductio without counter-thesis.
The Jain doctrine that reality is many-sided, so every assertion holds only in some respect.
The doctrine of ‘maybe’ or ‘in some respect’; the sevenfold scheme of conditioned predication.
Disputation: contending over whether a name fits a thing.
Rectification of names: making names fit realities and roles.
‘This is so’ / ‘this is not so’: the affirmations and denials of disputation, which Zhuangzi treats as indexical.
Dispute, especially halakhic disagreement among the Sages.
Paired study in which two learners argue through a text together.
Jewish law; the ruling followed in practice.
Dialectic or disputation, especially juridical disputation.
Formal disputation between a claimant and a questioner under fixed rules.
Independent juristic effort to derive a ruling from the sources.
Disagreement, especially legitimate disagreement among jurists.
A school of Islamic law.
The disputed question, the basic unit of scholastic teaching and writing.
The scholastic reply that separates two senses of a term, conceding the objection in one sense and denying it in the other.
In obligational disputation, the proposition the respondent is obliged to maintain.
Hegel’s term for a movement that at once cancels, preserves and raises what it overcomes.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if talks fail.
On this site, what a method of disagreement is for: truth, victory, formation, decision, settlement, understanding, plurality or release.
A conflict that cannot be fairly resolved because no rule of judgment applies to both sides.
A certainty that is not a conclusion but the axis on which doubting and judging turn.
In rationalist practice, a belief that would change your conclusion if it changed.
The strongest version of an opposing argument, the inverse of a straw man.
Selection of officials or deliberators by lot.
Habermas: the implicit claim to truth, rightness or sincerity raised by every speech act.
In formal dialectic, the running record of what each participant has committed to.
The sources of reasonable disagreement among people who are fully rational and in good faith.
Conflict between adversaries who share a framework, as against antagonism between enemies.

excerpts.text: War is father of all and king of all; and some he has shown as gods, others men; some he has made slaves, others free.

And what sort of difference creates enmity and anger? Suppose for example that you and I, my good friend, differ about a number; do differences of this sort make us enemies and set us at variance with one another? Do we not go at once to arithmetic, and put an end to them by a sum?

I am one of those who are very willing to be refuted if I say anything which is not true, and very willing to refute any one else who says what is not true, and quite as ready to be refuted as to refute; for I hold that this is the greater gain of the two.

Our treatise proposes to find a line of inquiry whereby we shall be able to reason from opinions that are generally accepted about every problem propounded to us, and also shall ourselves, when standing up to an argument, avoid saying anything that will obstruct us.
Scepticism is an ability to set out oppositions among things which appear and are thought of in any way at all.
If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things. If language be not in accordance with the truth of things, affairs cannot be carried on to success.

Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure; and one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure. Which is a dispute for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. And which is not for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Korah and all his company.
For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. … A Divine Voice emerged and proclaimed: Both these and those are the words of the living God. However, the halakha follows Beit Hillel.
If I had any thesis, that fault would apply to me. But I do not have any thesis.

And therefore, as when there is a controversy in an account, the parties must by their own accord set up for right reason the reason of some arbitrator, or judge, to whose sentence they will both stand, or their controversy must either come to blows, or be undecided, for want of a right reason constituted by Nature.

And though all the winds of doctrine were let loose to play upon the earth, so Truth be in the field, we do injuriously by licensing and prohibiting to misdoubt her strength. Let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?

The only way to rectify our reasonings is to make them as tangible as those of the Mathematicians, so that we can find our error at a glance, and when there are disputes among persons, we can simply say: Let us calculate, without further ado, to see who is right.
Real factions may be divided into those from interest, from principle, and from affection.
The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man. … But the most common and durable source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property.

He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. His reasons may be good, and no one may have been able to refute them. But if he is equally unable to refute the reasons on the opposite side; if he does not so much as know what they are, he has no ground for preferring either opinion.
The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.

To satisfy our doubts, therefore, it is necessary that a method should be found by which our beliefs may be determined by nothing human, but by some external permanency—by something upon which our thinking has no effect.

Where two principles really do meet which cannot be reconciled with one another, then each man declares the other a fool and heretic. I said I would ‘combat’ the other man,—but wouldn’t I give him reasons? Certainly; but how far do they go? At the end of reasons comes persuasion.
Each person can speak up for himself only after he has first restated the ideas and feelings of the previous speaker accurately, and to that speaker’s satisfaction.
As conflict—difference—is here in the world, as we cannot avoid it, we should, I think, use it.

sketch: Each party states a credence, not a verdict
Each estimates the other’s track record on similar questions
Both update by an agreed rule (equal weight, or weighted by record)
Record the result and score it later
peer.why: The epistemology of peer disagreement says what one should do on learning of disagreement, but no conversational practice enacts it.

sketch: Each side presents a solved problem it regards as a model of good work
Each tries to solve the other’s exemplar in its own terms
Map where the attempt breaks down
Treat the break as the boundary of translation, not as the opponent’s error
paradigm.why: Kuhn says persuasion across paradigms works through exemplars and conversion, not proof. No method trains it.

sketch: List every claim in the dispute
Mark each as belief (how things are) or attitude (what to favour)
Settle the belief claims by evidence
Negotiate or vote on the attitude claims, openly as such
attitude.why: Stevenson’s distinction is widely cited but rarely used as a procedure.

sketch: Identify the contested word
Ask what follows practically from each usage
Choose the usage whose consequences both can live with, or coin a new term
metaling.why: Conceptual engineering is a research programme but not yet a conversational method.

sketch: Each describes a shared event in their own final vocabulary
Each re-describes it in the other’s
Notice which words resist translation
Keep talking; aim for a third vocabulary, not a verdict
vocabularies.why: Rorty’s ironist redescribes, but he never wrote it down as a practice for two people.

sketch: Suspend the forum’s rules of evidence
Let the party who cannot state their wrong in the forum’s idiom try other idioms (story, image, silence)
Record what could not be said
Ask what idiom would be needed to judge it
differend.why: Lyotard’s remedy is to bear witness and to seek new idioms. Truth commissions came closest, but no general method exists.

sketch: Ask each side what may never be traded
Ask what gesture, such as apology, acknowledgement or ritual, would honour it
Exchange gestures before discussing material terms
sacred.why: Atran and Axelrod show that symbolic concessions move sacred-value conflicts. They give cases, not a protocol.

sketch: For each position, ask who gains materially if it prevails
Make the gains visible to both sides
Separate the material question from the ideological one and bargain over the first
class.why: Ideology critique is a method of analysis, not of conversation between the parties.

sketch: Each side lists what it shares with the other
Compare that list to what separates them
Ask what the dispute does for each group’s cohesion
small_diff.why: Freud diagnosed the pattern but proposed no talking cure for groups.

sketch: Name the object both parties want
Ask whose desire each is imitating
Name any third party being blamed by both
Refuse the scapegoat explicitly
mimetic.why: Girard’s theory implies renunciation of rivalry, but there is no practice for two rivals to do it together.

sketch: Assemble a group that genuinely disagrees
Each produces arguments; each evaluates the others’
Pool the evaluations, not the productions
argumentative.why: Mercier and Sperber show groups reason well under these conditions. The conditions are known; a named practice is not.

sketch: Each asks the other what they could not bear to be wrong about
Each identifies the system they are defending
Each tries to hold that system as an object for a while
developmental.why: Kegan’s developmental account explains why some conflicts cannot be resolved at a given order of mind, but it offers no method for two people at different orders.

sketch: Map the cleavages that divide a group
Deliberately build teams across them
Let conflict on one axis bind people allied on another
